hints: Look at how the carbon skeleton changes, the chain grows from 3 carbons to 4 carbons in the first step.
To replace $\text{Br}$ with $\text{CN}$ you need a good source of free cyanide ions, $\text{CN}^-$ for nucleophilic substitution.
Consider what hydrolyses a nitrile, $\text{-CN}$, all the way to a carboxylic acid, $\text{-COOH}$, rather than to its salt.
walkthrough:
**Spot the chain extension**

Great start, count the carbons. 1-bromopropane has 3 carbons, but butanenitrile and butanoic acid have 4 carbons.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$$

**Identify X for Br to CN**

This is nucleophilic substitution by $\text{CN}^-$. We need ionic cyanide dissolved in ethanol to favour substitution.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{CN}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN} + \text{Br}^-$$

**Identify Y for nitrile to acid**

Nitriles are hydrolysed by heating with dilute aqueous acid to give the carboxylic acid directly. Heating with alkali would give the carboxylate salt instead.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH} + \text{NH}_4^+$$

options.A: Ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$, would give a primary amine, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$, by nucleophilic substitution, not a nitrile. It cannot add the extra carbon needed.
options.B: X is correct here, but Y is wrong. Heating a nitrile with $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ gives the salt sodium butanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COO}^-\text{Na}^+$, not free butanoic acid. You would need a second acidification step.
options.C: X as $\text{KCN}$ in $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$ supplies $\text{CN}^-$ for substitution to form butanenitrile. Y as $\text{HCl(aq)}$ with heat gives acid hydrolysis of the nitrile to butanoic acid directly. This matches both steps perfectly.
options.D: $\text{HCN}$ is used for addition to carbonyls (aldehydes and ketones), not for substitution of a halogenoalkane, where $\text{KCN}$ is needed. $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ would also stop at the carboxylate salt, not the acid.
